name: Emperor Gaozong of Tang
extract:
Emperor Gaozong of Tang (21 July 628 – 27 December 683), personal name Li Zhi, was the third emperor of the Chinese Tang dynasty, ruling from 649 to 683; After January 665, he delegated a large portion of his power to his second wife, Empress Wu (the future Wu Zetian). Emperor Gaozong was the youngest son of Emperor Taizong and Empress Zhangsun; his elder brothers were Li Chengqian and Li Tai.
Emperor Gaozong of Tang, originally named Li Zhi, was born in the second year of the Zhenguan era (628). In the fifth year of Zhenguan (631), he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Jin. After Crown Prince Li Chengqian and the Prince of Wei, Li Tai, were successively deposed, Li Zhi was appointed Crown Prince in the seventeenth year of Zhenguan (643) with the support of his uncle, Zhangsun Wuji. In the twenty-third year of Zhenguan (649), Emperor Taizong passed away, and Li Zhi ascended the throne as Emperor Gaozong.
At the beginning of his reign, Emperor Gaozong was assisted by Zhangsun Wuji and Chu Suiliang. He respected their advice and governed with consultation, humility, and diligence, leading to a period of prosperity and stability that continued the achievements of the Zhenguan era. This period became known as the “Yonghui Reign of Peace.” At that time, Zhangsun Wuji’s authority cast a heavy shadow over the emperor, and both within and outside the court, everyone acted in accordance with his influence. Zhangsun Wuji fully followed the path of the former Emperor Taizong. All of this caused the emperor to be overshadowed both by the power of his minister and by the great legacy of his father, which gradually became a source of his hidden resentment.
In the sixth year of the Yonghui era (655), Emperor Gaozong deposed  Empress Wang and established Wu Zetian as the new empress. This issue was not merely a matter of family disputes or harem intrigue; rather, it reflected a power struggle between the Guanzhong (Guanlong) faction and the Shandong faction. The deposition and appointment of empresses initiated a new balance among factions—namely, the breakdown of the Guanzhong aristocratic monopoly on power, the consolidation of authority in the hands of the emperor, and the advancement of commoners within the state bureaucracy. Empress Wu played a crucial role in all of these developments. In the second year of the Xianqing era (657), he designated Luoyang as the Eastern Capital in order to solve grain transportation and supply problems.
After the deaths of his senior ministers, Emperor Gaozong gradually became more autocratic, rejecting criticism and suppressing dissent. Political authority shifted from collective consultation among senior ministers to a small private circle of trusted individuals within the inner palace. As a result, anyone who gained close access to the emperor could acquire extraordinary power and influence. Officials inside and outside the court became afraid to speak openly, allowing flatterers to gain influence while loyal and capable ministers were marginalized. Historians later criticized this change, saying that “the achievements of the earlier worthy ruler were undone by the later foolishness.”
At the same time, Emperor Gaozong initiated large-scale construction projects and imposed heavy corvée labor on the population. As a result, the people suffered greatly, and dissatisfaction spread throughout the empire. 
Emperor Gaozong's reign also witnessed the rise and primacy of Empress Wu, who became the effective power behind the Tang rule. Empress Wu aided Emperor Gaozong in his rule during the later years of his reign after a series of strokes left him incapacitated. From the fifth year of the Xianqing era (660), Emperor Gaozong began suffering from illness, described as headaches,  dizziness, heaviness in the head, and impaired vision; unfortunately, he never recovered, and as he grew older, the progression of his illness became more severe. Because of his declining health, he increasingly entrusted state affairs to Empress Wu, who began administering government matters from within the inner palace, or, at times when the emperor personally responded to memorials submitted by officials, she had already summarized them for him and assisted him in reading and analyzing them. Whenever the emperor held court thereafter, she attended from behind a curtain behind the throne, hearing and observing the discussions and participating in affairs of state. She was an intelligent and quick-witted woman, skilled in strategy and tactics, and also knowledge of literature and history. From then on, Empress Wu made her prestige and authority equal to that of the emperor: over time, accumulated extensive experience in governance and political maneuvering, ranging from employing talented individuals to eliminating her opponents. This period became known as the “Two Sages Administering the Court Together” (二圣临朝, Èr Shèng Lín Cháo).
Emperor Gaozong gradually ceased to involve himself in the intricate details of state affairs. However, he formally retained authority over major matters throughout his lifetime, including the appointment and dismissal of chancellors, issuing judgments in serious criminal cases (including capital offenses), designating the crown prince, and making decisions regarding war and peace. However, even when he personally handled these matters, he would consult Empress Wu, or—due to his illness or indecision—delegate them to her for decision-making. Gradually, Empress Wu began acting more independently, shaping decisions according to her own interests, and exercising the power of reward and punishment. At first, she relied on the emperor, but over time she did so without his knowledge. This increasingly displeased Emperor Gaozong, leading him in 664 to consult with the chancellor Shangguan Yi and secretly plan her removal. However, Empress Wu soon learned of the plot and swiftly moved to stop it. Shangguan Yi, along with many associates connected to the former Crown Prince Li Zhong, was subsequently accused of conspiring against the emperor and executed. These events became known as the “Shangguan Yi Incident.” 
From this point onward, the empress’s authority grew even stronger. At the same time, however, she became more cautious and politically calculated, placing greater emphasis on securing legitimacy for her position and consolidating her power in a more stable and sustainable manner. In the final years of emperor's life—roughly the last eight or nine years of his reign after 674—the emperor reportedly considered abdication several times. Most notably, he once contemplated transferring power to the empress, but faced opposition. Following the sudden and suspicious death of Crown Prince Li Hong in 675, Li Xián, succeeded his brother as heir apparent. Li Xián later came under increasing scrutiny for demonstrating independence and political competence. At the same time, rumors circulating within the court questioned his legitimacy as the son of the empress, further fueled by suspicions that the empress herself may have been involved in the alleged poisoning of the previous crown prince. As a result, the relationship between mother and son deteriorated severely.
In particular, as the emperor’s health worsened, the issue of succession became increasingly urgent. Empress Wu, unwilling to relinquish power and determined to secure absolute authority for the period after Emperor Gaozong, began laying the groundwork for the removal of the crown prince. In 680, Li Xián was accused of plotting a coup, stripped of his title, reduced to the status of a commoner, and exiled and imprisoned. From that point onward, no one was able to effectively challenge the empress’s authority. 
After Emperor Gaozong died in December 683, power passed entirely into the hands of Empress Wu. As Empress Dowager and regent, she “presided over court and issued edicts” (臨朝稱制; lin chao chengzhi), effectively governing in place of the emperor. She in turn deposed and installed her two sons, Emperors Zhongzong and Ruizong; she removed the former for showing signs of independence, and kept the latter effectively under house arrest throughout his nominal reign. In the following years, she consolidated her authority through a series of comprehensive reforms, extensive political purges at all levels, eliminating rivals both within and outside the court, and by orchestrating a propaganda campaign based on celestial omens to legitimize her rule, thereby securing undisputed control over the state. Ultimately, she formally established her own dynasty, the Zhou, replacing the Tang, and became the only woman in Chinese history to rule as an empress regnant. After his death, he was interred at the Qian Mausoleum along with Wu Zetian.
During the first part of his reign, Tang territorial gains, which started with his father Emperor Taizong, continued, including the conquest of Baekje, Goguryeo, and the Western Turkic Khaganate, but throughout the 670s, much of those gains were lost to the Tibetan Empire, Silla, Khitans, and Balhae. Further, territory previously conquered that belonged to both the Göktürks and the Western Turkic Khaganate were subjected to repeated rebellions.
The personality of Emperor Gaozong, when examined beyond the one-sided judgments of early historians, can be described as follows: he was an intelligent but not a genius ruler, someone with willpower but not exceptional decisiveness, and a moderately successful administrator who appears less prominent when placed alongside extraordinary figures such as Emperor Taizong and Wu Zetian. Many of the weaknesses attributed to him stem from comparisons with these two highly exceptional figures rather than necessarily from his own inherent incompetence. One of his major problems was his poor health, which began to seriously affect him from the middle of his reign and gradually worsened until the end of his life. Historians who judged him as being under the control of his wife and as having delegated state affairs to her should be viewed more rationally, since he had little alternative—entrusting his duties to ministers would have been even more dangerous. Moreover, he made several attempts to prepare his sons, Li Hong and Li Xian, for succession by assigning them various responsibilities, but fate or Empress Wu’s ambition prevented this goal from being realized. At the time of his death, he left a will stating that his successor, Li Zhe (later known as Emperor Zhongzong), should immediately ascend the throne in front of his coffin. However, major unresolved state affairs and political dilemmas were entrusted to Empress Wu’s decision. Empress Wu then delayed the enthronement ceremony of her son and, with the support of officials, formally assumed the regency. From that point onward, subsequent developments unfolded.
